631.title: Many rooms (John 14:1–7)
631.hook: let not your heart be troubled; in my Father's house are many rooms
631.carry: let not your heart be troubled
631.howItsDone: Christians often read these words at funerals and memorial services, and some also pray "let not your heart be troubled" in times of worry.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new commandment: love one another as I have loved you, the sentence behind Maundy Thursday. Your line was by this, all will know. What visible love did you show? Day six hundred thirty-one.

Some houses keep a room ready. The bed made up. A towel on the end of it. Someone thought of the guest before the guest arrived. Now go back to that supper table. Judas has gone. Jesus has just told Peter he'll deny him. He's said he's leaving, and they can't come yet. The room is full of fear. Their whole lives have been built around following this man for years. And the first thing he says to them is about their hearts.

"Let not your heart be troubled: ye believe in God, believe also in me." Remember, a few days ago Jesus himself said, now is my soul troubled. He knows the feeling from inside. He isn't scolding them for being afraid. He's giving them somewhere to put the fear. Then: "In my Father's house are many mansions: if it were not so, I would have told you. I go to prepare a place for you." Mansions sounds like big estates on a hill. But in the English of the King James Bible, a mansion simply meant a dwelling place, somewhere you stay. The Greek word is monē, from a verb meaning to remain, to abide. That same verb will be all over the next chapter: abide in me. So the picture isn't a gated community. It's a big family house with room for everyone, a place to stay and not have to leave. And many rooms: no shortage, no waiting list. And Jesus goes ahead to get them ready, like someone making up the bed before a guest arrives. Thomas says it plainly: "Lord, we know not whither thou goest; and how can we know the way?" And Jesus answers: "I am the way, the truth, and the life: no man cometh unto the Father, but by me." Christians hold this line at the center of their faith in Jesus. Churches have long talked about what it means for people of other paths, and they don't all answer it the same way. For Thomas, at that table, it meant: you don't need a map. You need me.
screen: `THOMAS: HOW CAN WE KNOW THE WAY?`
then, large: `LET NOT YOUR HEART BE TROUBLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: prepare a room or a bed for a guest. If you can, get up and tidy a corner, a couch, a chair where someone could sit. If you can't move right now, picture a room in your home. Settle, and breathe. Imagine who might come: a friend, a relative, a stranger who needs somewhere to stay. Picture making it ready. Clean sheets, a glass of water, a light left on. Think of the care that goes into a room prepared ahead. If you pray, you can give thanks for a place made ready for you. If you don't, simply enjoy the thought of welcoming someone. The bell holds the time.
Many rooms. Jesus's promise at the supper: in my Father's house are many dwelling places, and he goes ahead to prepare one.
Your line: let not your heart be troubled. Today, when worry rises, say the line once, and then make one small space ready for someone else. Day six hundred thirty-one.

632.title: Show us the Father (John 14:8–21)
632.hook: Philip asks, and he says: whoever has seen me has seen the Father
632.howItsDone: John 14 is often read at Christian funerals and in the Easter season, and Christians hear in Jesus's reply to Philip a claim at the center of their faith: that in Jesus, God is made known.

segments.voice: Yesterday, many rooms in the Father's house, and a table where the friends were troubled. Your line was let not your heart be troubled. Did you make room for someone? Day six hundred thirty-two.

Philip is the practical one. Back in chapter six, with a hungry crowd on a hillside, about five thousand men by John's count, Philip was the one who did the math: two hundred pennyworth of bread wouldn't be enough. Now it's the last supper, and Jesus has been talking for a while about going to the Father, about the way, about knowing the Father already. And Philip, still at the table, says the plain thing. Enough talk. Just show us. One look, and we'll be satisfied. It's a very honest request. Today, the answer he gets.

In the King James Bible Philip says: "Lord, shew us the Father, and it sufficeth us." It sufficeth us: that would do it. And the reply comes with a little ache in it: "Have I been so long time with you, and yet hast thou not known me, Philip? he that hath seen me hath seen the Father." All those meals and roads and boats, and Philip is still waiting for the real thing to show up. The answer is that it already has. Hold that up against the Hebrew Bible for a moment. Moses once asked to see God's glory, and in Exodus he is told no one can see God's face and live. In its first chapter, John's Gospel struck the same note: no one has seen God at any time, and the Son has made him known. So when Philip asks to see, the Gospel's answer is a person at a table. Watch how he washes feet, who he eats with, how he speaks to a grieving sister: John's claim is that this is what God is like. Christians have built a great deal on this line. Churches that teach the Trinity read it alongside their teaching that the Father and the Son are distinct and yet one God, and theologians have worked long and hard on how to say that well. The turn is there in the scene itself, though. Philip wants a vision in the sky. He's offered a face across the table. Then Jesus promises he won't leave them orphans. The King James says it this way: "I will not leave you comfortless: I will come to you." Another helper is coming, he says, who will stay with them. That thread comes back in the days ahead.
screen: `SHOW US THE FATHER, AND IT'S ENOUGH.`
`SO LONG WITH YOU, AND YOU DON'T KNOW ME?`
`NO ONE HAS SEEN GOD; THE SON MAKES HIM KNOWN.`
then, large: `HE THAT HATH SEEN ME HATH SEEN THE FATHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for God's face in kindness. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one scene from the Gospels where Jesus is kind. Washing the disciples' feet. Bending down to write in the dirt. Calling a short man down from a tree. Pick one and let it play slowly. Watch his hands. Watch who he looks at. If you're a Christian, this is what the line says God looks like. If you're learning, simply notice what kind of face the Gospel is describing. If you pray, you can hold that scene before God in silence. The bell holds the time.
Show us the Father. Philip's honest request, and the answer: whoever has seen Jesus has seen the Father.
Your line: seen the father. Today, when someone is kind to you, pause and notice what that kindness shows you about the one who gave it. Day six hundred thirty-two.

633.title: My peace I give you (John 14:22–31)
633.howItsDone: In many churches, Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, Methodist and others, the congregation shares the peace during the service, turning to neighbors with a handshake or embrace and the words peace be with you.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Philip said show us the Father, and heard that he already had. Your line was seen the father. What kindness did you notice? Day six hundred thirty-three.

A ring. A recipe card. A watch. At a hospital bed or an airport gate, when a goodbye is serious, people often skip the speech. They hand over one small thing, something to hold when the person isn't there. At the last supper, Jesus knows he's leaving. A second Judas at the table, not Iscariot, has just asked him a question. And Jesus answers, and then he does what people do at goodbyes. He leaves them something. Not an object. Today, what he gave.
screen: `AT A GOODBYE, PEOPLE GIVE ONE THING.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid." Notice it's a bequest. I leave with you: the language of someone settling what they're handing on. The Greek word is eirene, and behind it stands the Hebrew shalom, which Jews used, and still use, as a greeting and a goodbye. Shalom is more than quiet. It carries the sense of wholeness, everything in its right place, nothing missing. So in one way this is the ordinary farewell any Jewish teacher might give his friends. And then he adds the strange part: not as the world giveth. How does the world give peace? Usually by removing the problem. Pay the bill, end the argument, win the war, then you can relax. Jesus is about to be arrested. Nothing is being removed. The peace he offers comes in the middle of the trouble, not after it. He also promises a helper, the Holy Ghost, who will teach them and bring to their remembrance everything he said. They won't be left to remember on their own. Then the chapter ends with an odd line: "Arise, let us go hence." Let's go. And yet he keeps talking for three more chapters before they leave. Readers have long puzzled over that. Some think the Gospel was edited in stages; others think they rose and he went on speaking as they walked. The text doesn't say. In some churches the gift comes back every week: at the passing of the peace, people turn to the person next to them and say, peace be with you.
screen: `A GOODBYE GIFT: PEACE I LEAVE WITH YOU.`
`ARISE, LET US GO, AND HE KEEPS TALKING.`
then, large: `MY PEACE I GIVE UNTO YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pass peace to someone. Settle, and breathe. Notice one trouble you're carrying right now, and don't try to solve it. Just let it be there. Now, in the middle of it, breathe slower. That's the shape of the peace in this chapter: not after the trouble, but inside it. Then think of one person who's carrying something heavy. Picture them. If you pray, you can say his words for them: peace I leave with you. If you don't, simply wish them wholeness. The bell holds the time.
My peace I give you. A goodbye gift, the old word shalom: wholeness offered in the middle of trouble, not after it.
screen: `MY PEACE I GIVE YOU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not as the world gives. Today, send one message or say one sentence that passes peace to someone who's carrying something heavy. Day six hundred thirty-three.

634.title: I am the vine (John 15:1–8)
634.hook: abide in me; the branch can't bear fruit alone
634.howItsDone: Christians speak of abiding in Christ through prayer, scripture, worship and, in many churches, Communion.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a goodbye gift: my peace I give unto you. Your line was not as the world gives. Who did you pass peace to? Day six hundred thirty-four.

Cut a branch off a grapevine and lay it on the kitchen counter. For a day it looks fine. Green leaves, maybe a few small grapes. You could put it in a vase and fool a guest. By the end of the week it's curling and brown. Nothing went wrong with the branch itself. It just isn't attached to anything anymore. Anyone who tended vines knew this. And the vine was an old picture for Israel itself in the Psalms and the prophets. So when Jesus reaches for an image on his last night, he picks one the people at the table would have known well.
screen: `A CUT BRANCH LOOKS FINE FOR A DAY.`
`THE VINE: AN OLD PICTURE FOR ISRAEL.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the husbandman." Husbandman is an old word for farmer, here the vinedresser who prunes. Then the center of the passage: "Abide in me, and I in you. As the branch cannot bear fruit of itself, except it abide in the vine; no more can ye, except ye abide in me." Abide. The Greek verb is meno: to stay, to remain, to live somewhere and not leave. John comes back to it again and again. In the first chapter, two disciples asked Jesus where he was staying, and they came and stayed with him that day. Same verb. And here, in a few short verses, the verb keeps coming back, like a refrain. Notice what Jesus does not say. He doesn't say try harder to produce fruit. Branches don't strain. Fruit is simply what happens when the sap gets through. The work is staying attached. There's also a harder edge: the farmer prunes. Branches that bear fruit are cut back so they'll bear more, and branches cut off from the vine wither and are gathered and burned. Christians read that pruning in different ways: as discipline, as loss that leads to growth, or as the warning it sounds like. Some readers find comfort in it too. A vinedresser cuts because he expects a harvest. Then the line that sums it up: "I am the vine, ye are the branches." Not I am the trunk and you hang off me somewhere. One plant.
screen: `I AM THE TRUE VINE; MY FATHER, THE FARMER.`
`MENO: TO STAY, TO REMAIN, TO LIVE THERE.`
then, large: `I AM THE VINE, YE ARE THE BRANCHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay connected to what feeds you. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself what actually feeds you. Not what distracts you or fills the time. What sends life through you? A friendship. Prayer. Music. Scripture. A long walk. A table with people you love. Find one. Now notice how long it's been since you were really connected to it. Don't scold yourself. Just stay with it for these minutes, the way a branch stays on a vine. If you pray, you can simply rest in the words abide in me. The bell holds the time.
Abide. In Greek, meno: to stay, to remain, to make your home somewhere. The branch's whole job, in John's picture, is to stay attached.
Your line: abide. Today, give fifteen minutes to the one thing that feeds you, and don't rush back. Day six hundred thirty-four.

635.title: I have called you friends (John 15:9–17)
635.hook: greater love has no one than this
635.howItsDone: Many Christians speak of Jesus as a friend in prayer and in hymns, and John 15:13 is read at many memorial services for people who died serving others.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the vine and the branches. Your word was abide: stay, remain, don't leave. What did you stay connected to? Day six hundred thirty-five.

It's late on the last night, and the supper is nearly over. Jesus is talking to eleven friends, a few hours before his arrest, and he says a line that would end up carved on war memorials and on plaques for soldiers, firefighters and nurses: greater love hath no man than this. People reach for it when someone has given their life for others. But at the table it was said about friendship. And the sentence that comes right after it is just as surprising.

Here's the line in full, in the King James Bible: "Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends." For his friends. That word is the key to the whole passage. Jesus has just repeated the commandment he gave earlier that same evening: love one another, as I have loved you. Then he names what they are to him. "Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends." Think about what that meant in that world. A servant follows orders and isn't told the reasons. A friend is let in on the plan. And Jesus says that's the difference: all things that I have heard of my Father I have made known unto you. The Greek word is philoi, friends, from the same family as philos, loved one. In the Hebrew Bible, very few people get called God's friend. Abraham is one, in Isaiah and in Chronicles. Of Moses, Exodus says God spoke with him face to face, as a man speaks to his friend. So this is a big word to hand to eleven ordinary men, fishermen and a tax collector among them. Then one more turn: "Ye have not chosen me, but I have chosen you." In those days students usually picked their teacher. Here the teacher did the picking. Christians hear two things in this passage, and they hold them together. One is comfort: being chosen, being let in, being called friend. The other is the cost: a friendship measured by a life laid down. Many Christians see that measure fulfilled the next day, at the cross.
screen: `A SERVANT ISN'T TOLD; A FRIEND IS.`
`YE HAVE NOT CHOSEN ME; I CHOSE YOU.`
then, large: `I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do a friend's favor. Settle, and breathe. Think of a friend, and think of something they need that you could actually do. Not a grand gesture. Picking up their kid. Proofreading their resume. Returning the dish. Listening to the long story again. Picture yourself doing it, and doing it the way a friend does, not like a servant ticking a box. Then think of one person who has done that for you, and let yourself be grateful. If you pray, you can give thanks for them by name. The bell holds the time.
I have called you friends. Not servants who follow orders without knowing why, but friends who are let in on the plan.
screen: `I HAVE CALLED YOU FRIENDS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: not servants, friends. Today, do the favor you pictured, before the day ends, and do it as a friend. Day six hundred thirty-five.

636.title: If the world hates you (John 15:18–27)
636.hook: a warning that following him won't always be popular
636.howItsDone: Christians in places where faith brings danger often read John 15 as words of courage, and some churches set aside a day each year to pray for Christians who are persecuted.

segments.voice: Yesterday, greater love, and a new name: I have called you friends. Your line was not servants, friends. Did you do the favor? Day six hundred thirty-six.

Most recruiting pitches lead with the good news. Join us: great team, real purpose, benefits from day one. The hard parts come later, in the fine print, if at all. Jesus has just told his friends they are chosen, loved, let in on the plan. And then, in the very same breath, he does something no recruiter would do. He tells them the hard part. Plainly, at the table, with no fine print. People will not always like you for this. Some will hate you. Today, the warning.
screen: `RECRUITERS SAVE THE HARD PART FOR LATER.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you." The world here is the Greek word kosmos. And John uses it in a surprising double way. In chapter three, God so loved the world. Here, the world hates. Same word. Here the world seems to mean not the planet or nature or ordinary life, but people and powers organized as if God weren't there. In John's telling, God loves it, and it often doesn't love back. So the warning isn't that the disciples should hate the world. It's that they shouldn't be shocked when the world pushes against them. Then Jesus reminds them of something he said at the foot washing: "The servant is not greater than his lord." If they treated me this way, he says, don't expect better. And he quotes a line of scripture, one readers find in the Psalms: "They hated me without a cause." There's a comfort folded inside the warning, and it's in that small word before. It hated me before it hated you. The disciples won't be the first; he has gone through it ahead of them. The passage ends with a promise and a job. The Comforter, the Spirit of truth, will testify, and so will they, "because ye have been with me from the beginning." Christians have read these verses in very different times. Where believers have faced real persecution, in the early centuries and in places today, the words have been a lifeline. In comfortable places, some readers take them as a warning against two things: seeking approval at any cost, and mistaking ordinary criticism for persecution.
screen: `THE SERVANT IS NOT GREATER THAN HIS LORD.`
`IT HATED ME FIRST: HE WENT AHEAD.`
`THE SPIRIT TESTIFIES, AND SO WILL YOU.`
then, large: `IT HATED ME BEFORE IT HATED YOU.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stay kind when disliked. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who doesn't like you. A coworker, an in-law, a neighbor, someone online. Notice what happens in your body when you picture them. The tight jaw, the speech you're already rehearsing. Breathe into that. Now picture one small kindness you could show them anyway. Not to win them over. Just because kindness doesn't need their approval. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
If the world hates you. A plain warning at the table: following him won't always be popular, and he went through it first.
screen: `IF THE WORLD HATES YOU — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: it hated me first. Today, when someone is cold to you, answer with one small kindness, and let it stand without needing a reply. Day six hundred thirty-six.

637.title: The Spirit of truth (John 16:1–15)
637.hook: the Advocate will guide you into all truth
637.howItsDone: Christians often pray for the Holy Spirit's guidance before decisions, meetings and the reading of scripture, and many churches celebrate the Spirit's coming at Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a warning with no fine print. Your line was it hated me first. Were you able to stay kind to someone cold? Day six hundred thirty-seven.

An ancient courtroom. You've been accused, and you're standing alone. Then someone walks in and stands beside you. Not the judge. Not a hired gun who talks over you. A friend of good standing who comes alongside and speaks up for you. The Greeks had a word for that person. Jesus has just told his friends that the world may turn against them. Now he tells them who will be standing beside them when it does.

The word is parakletos. Para means beside, and kletos means called: one called to your side. In a courtroom, that's an advocate. The King James Bible translates it Comforter, and in older English, comfort carried a sense of strengthening, not only soothing. Other translations say Helper, Counselor, Advocate. No single English word holds it all, and that's why some people simply say Paraclete. Here's the surprising part. Jesus tells his friends it's good that he's leaving. "It is expedient for you that I go away: for if I go not away, the Comforter will not come unto you." Expedient means better for you. They can't imagine that. Then he admits something tender: "I have yet many things to say unto you, but ye cannot bear them now." He doesn't dump everything on them at once. And then the promise in today's carry: "when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth." Guide. The Greek word has the sense of leading someone along a way. Not dropping all the answers at once, but walking you there. Christians understand this promise in several ways. Catholic and Orthodox Christians see the Spirit guiding the whole church through its teaching and tradition over the centuries. Many Protestants emphasize the Spirit opening the scriptures to believers as they read. Pentecostal Christians speak of the Spirit's guidance as close and present, in daily life.
